headline: wholesale is still high and storage is thin - but switching has slowed, so suppliers are pricing keenly to win new business
commentary:
UK power spot is 147.31 £/MWh, up 94% on a year ago and just below the 153.00 high logged last week. The week's fall had a specific cause: reports that Saudi Arabia is working to bring its East-West crude pipeline back into service took part of the outage premium out of oil, and the UK gas front month closed below 192 p/therm for three consecutive sessions before rebounding 3.3% on Friday to 197.06.

We would not read that as the market turning. Oct 26 at 197.06 is still marginally above the 195.59 of 9 September, and the structural position has not improved: European gas storage sits at roughly 68% of capacity, near two-decade lows, after a summer of disrupted Gulf LNG and record heat, with Asian buyers competing for the same cargoes once the cold arrives.

The more useful point is that wholesale sets the floor, not the price you pay. High prices have slowed switching right across the market - businesses are reluctant to fix at a peak - but suppliers still have books to fill, and the one thing they control is their own margin. Across the tenders we are running now, that shows up in the spread: quoted on the same meters on the same day, against the same wholesale cost, the gap between the best and worst offer is unusually wide. That part of your bill is winnable today, whichever way the curve moves next, and it is exactly what the comparison on this page is measuring.

For context on the volatility a fixed price removes: day-ahead power averaged 32.71 £/MWh on Saturday 19 September, dipping below zero at midday, against a peak hour of 204.69 five days earlier.

gas.note: NBP front-month (Oct 26) is 197.06 p/therm, and the whole of next winter sits alongside it rather than above it - Winter 26 197.50, Dec 26 200.75, Jan 27 200.98. Then the curve falls off a cliff. Each of the next two winters is priced roughly a third below the one before: Winter 26 197.50, Winter 27 129.00 (-34.7%), Winter 28 89.50 (-30.6%), or -54.7% across the two years. Summer 27 is 134.01. That shape is the whole case for term - a 24-month contract blends next winter's prices down with materially cheaper 2027 and 2028, and a 36-month reaches the third step. Note the Winter 26 to Winter 27 discount has NARROWED from 38.3% four days ago to 34.7%, because the prompt gave back its outage premium while 2027 barely moved: last week's mechanism running in reverse, a physical outage pricing into the front and so does its relief. Winter 27 has now held between 123.75 and 130.25 across five readings, which is why the term argument is anchored on it.
